query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing Hf with Nb in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its overall density while retaining its high strength at both room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr, with a density of about 10.21 g/cm³ and demonstrated high mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Substitute the heavy Hf element with the lighter refractory element Nb, thereby forming an NbMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperature (around 1000 °C) under similar loading conditions as the original alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and retention of a single-phase solid solution that provides solid solution strengthening and phase stability similar to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.mechanism: By replacing Hf (a heavy element with an atomic weight near 178) with Nb (a lighter refractory element with an atomic weight near 93), the overall alloy density is reduced. If the atomic size mismatch and mixing entropy continue to favor the formation of a stable solid solution, the intrinsic strengthening mechanisms (such as lattice distortion induced solid solution strengthening) can be maintained at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The NbMoTaTiZr alloy should exhibit a lower density than 10.21 g/cm³ while retaining or closely matching the mechanical strength and high-temperature performance of the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy properties: high strength at room temperature and at ~1000 °C, with a density of 10.21 g/cm³.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under as-cast processing conditions and within the temperature range of room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C. Mechanical loading should mimic conditions used in previous evaluations of similar refractory high-entropy alloys.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding how the removal of Hf might affect the finer details of the alloy’s solid solution strengthening and phase stability. The full impact of atomic size mismatches and potential formation of secondary phases after substitution needs experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the NbMoTaTiZr alloy (with Hf fully replaced by Nb) using the same as-cast processing methods. Characterize its phase structure (using XRD and microscopy), measure density, and perform mechanical tests (such as tensile/compressive tests) at room temperature and around 1000 °C. Compare these results directly with the properties of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
measurements: Room temperature tensile and yield strength tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NbMoTaTiZr alloy either (a) shows a significant drop in mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength, yield strength) at room temperature or at 1000 °C compared to the HfMoTaTiZr alloy, or (b) does not maintain a single-phase solid solution (e.g., develops brittle secondary phases) despite the reduced density, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
